content: The 7 + 3 chemotherapy regimen is a widely used first-line induction therapy for acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), excluding the acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) subtype. APL is better treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and/or arsenic trioxide, which often require little to no chemotherapy. The name 7 + 3 refers to the treatment schedule: seven days of standard-dose cytarabine and three days of an anthracycline antibiotic or anthracenedione, most commonly daunorubicin. Daunorubicin can be substituted with doxorubicin, idarubicin, or mitoxantrone. The standard 7 + 3 regimen involves: Seven days of cytarabine combined with three days of daunorubicin. Alternatively, seven days of cytarabine with three days of idarubicin. Another variation includes seven days of cytarabine with three days of mitoxantrone. Attempts have been made to intensify the 7 + 3 regimen to improve its efficacy. These efforts included extending the duration of cytarabine to 10 days or increasing the duration of daunorubicin or idarubicin to 4–5 days. However, these modifications often resulted in increased toxicity without significant improvement in outcomes. Conversely, reducing the dose or duration of the regimen to minimize toxicity compromised its effectiveness. The addition of vinca alkaloids, such as vincristine or vinblastine, to the 7 + 3 regimen was historically popular in AML treatment. However, this approach proved harmful, as vinca alkaloids are rapidly inactivated in myeloid cells by the enzyme myeloperoxidase. This inactivation leads to greater damage to lymphoid cells, including T-cells responsible for antileukemic immunity, than to myeloid cells. Furthermore, vinca alkaloids induce cell cycle arrest in AML cells, rendering them less sensitive to cytarabine and anthracyclines. Similarly, the addition of glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisolone), methotrexate, or alkylating agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide or melphalan) to the 7 + 3 regimen has shown no benefit in AML treatment. The addition of etoposide to the standard 7 + 3 regimen has demonstrated some benefit in poor-risk AML patients, particularly those who are refractory to standard induction regimens. This combination gave rise to the ADE (or DAE) regimen, which includes daunorubicin, cytarabine, and etoposide. Unlike combinations with vinca alkaloids or prednisolone, the ADE regimen is still occasionally used in poor-risk AML patients. Other variations of the 7 + 3 regimen include the addition of thioguanine, resulting in the DAT regimen, and the addition of 6-mercaptopurine, leading to the DAM regimen.
